Ahead of next week's High-Level Political Forum, the latest Tracking SDG 7: The Energy Progress Report offers an important snapshot of where the global energy transition stands—and why this may be one of the greatest development opportunities of our time.
 
The numbers tell a story that goes well beyond the remaining challenges.
Since the SDGs were adopted in 2015, the number of people living without electricity has fallen from 958 million to 655 million. Renewable energy has grown by 79% since 2013, now accounting for 18% of global final energy consumption and more than 30% of global electricity generation. Installed renewable energy capacity has more than doubled—from 248 watts per person in 2015 to 544 watts per person in 2024—while international public finance supporting clean energy in developing countries has increased from USD 14.3 billion to USD 24.6 billion.
 
Yet if we look beyond the numbers, an even more important story is emerging.
 
The world is not facing the same energy transition we imagined in 2015. Geopolitical uncertainty, shifting supply chains, climate risks and the rapid rise of AI are fundamentally reshaping energy systems. But these changes are also creating unprecedented incentives to accelerate the transition.
Today, investing in clean energy is no longer driven only by climate ambition. It is increasingly about energy security, economic competitiveness, industrial development and resilience.
 
At the same time, digitalization and AI are creating new opportunities to build smarter grids, improve energy efficiency, integrate renewables and expand access to affordable and reliable energy.
 
Accelerating renewable energy deployment and energy efficiency strengthens energy security, reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels and enhances macroeconomic resilience, particularly in developing countries.
Important gaps remain. 645 million people are still projected to remain without electricity by 2030, nearly 2 billion people continue to rely on polluting cooking fuels, and globally only 22% of households without electricity can afford a basic electricity connection.
 
Universal access will require us to more than triple the current pace of progress.
 
As the final in-depth review of SDG 7 before 2030, this year's High-Level Political Forum is an opportunity not only to assess progress, but to redefine the just energy transition as one of the strongest drivers of development, resilience, prosperity and peace in an increasingly uncertain world.
